newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deng death leaves Asia currency traders unmoved.
newsitem.headline: Deng death leaves Asia currency traders unmoved.

text.p: The overnight death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping left foreign exchange dealers in Asia unmoved on Thursday and the markets showed hardly any reaction.
"As far as the foreign exchange market is concerned Deng's been dead for two or three years anyway," commented the head of Treasury at a European bank in Singapore.
At 0215 GMT the U.S. dollar was quoted at 1.6900/10 marks, virtually at the low of the day. It ended in New York on Wednesday at 1.6975/85.
Investors usually flock to buy 'safe haven' U.S. dollars at times of political turmoil and instability but dealers said there was no sign of any panic buying.
"On a boredom scale of one to ten, today ranks as a 12. There's nothing happening," the chief foreign exchange trader at another European bank said.
"Deng was 92 and this was always going to happen. If you look at the Hong Kong dollar and the Chinese yuan, you'll see that they've actually gone up against the U.S. dollar today," he added.
The yuan opened at 8.2940 against the U.S. dollar in Shanghai compared with a close on Wednesday of 8.2945 and dealers there said investors had been psychologically prepared for Deng's death.
At 0230 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was trading at 7.7430/40 to the U.S. unit, around 50 basis points firmer on the day.

The head of Treasury at the European bank said the U.S. dollar had spiked up to hit a traded high of 1.7005 against the mark in New York shortly after confirmation that Deng had died was received by the market.
"That was just a classic knee-jerk reaction by New York. But here in Asia it's a case of 'buy the rumour, sell the fact'," he said.
It was unlikely the dollar would be affected much in the future since the market was assuming China's leadership was well-prepared for Deng's death, he added.

"I'm no expert on Chinese politics but unless things get really nasty -- in-fighting between opposing factions, troops on the streets, that sort of thing -- then you're not going to see much on the foreign exchange front," he said.

The chief foreign exchange trader agreed. Chinese President "Jiang Zemin seems to have his feet tucked securely under the desk and as long as this is the case, you won't see much in the way of reaction from us," he said.
A trader at a European bank commented, "I'm more interested in the living than the dead. (U.S. Federal Reserve chief Alan) Greenspan can move markets, but Deng can't."
